newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian Solvay reports flat H1 1997, CEO to retire.
newsitem.headline: Belgian Solvay reports flat H1 1997, CEO to retire.

text.p: Belgian chemicals group Solvay reported flat first-half 1997 earnings on Thursday and said it would not make any comment on second half prospects because the outlook for key businesses remained uncertain.
"We are not making any forecast for the second half or for the whole of the year," Solvay chief executive officer Daniel Janssen told a news conference.

Solvay said current earnings in the six months to June 30 rose three percent to 6.1 billion Belgian francs ($161 million), at the bottom end of analysts' expectations, as sharp declines in caustic soda and hydrogen peroxide prices wiped out a spectacular recovery in its plastics business.

Solvay said it had also not benefitted from currency movements, as gains from the rise in the U.S. dollar against the Belgian franc were offset by provisions on potential losses caused by the devaluation of the Thai baht.

Solvay holds 45 percent of Thai PVC maker Vinythai, whose debt is to a large part denominated in dollars, Janssen said. Further provisions might be needed at the end of 1997 should the baht slide below 32 to the dollar.

Publishing for the first time a half-year breakdown of sales and results of its main businesses, Solvay said earnings before debt interest and taxes (EBIT) in plastics rose 125 percent to 35 billion francs while EBIT in chemicals fell 39 percent to 3.7 billion francs.
Chemicals has since July 1 comprised Solvay's alkalis and peroxygens business, reducing the number of separate business units to four from five.
EBIT at the other two units, plastics processing and pharmaceuticals, was unchanged at 1.3 and 2.0 billion francs respectively.

Solvay noted that if the sale last year of its animal health business was stripped out of the figures, like-for-like EBIT in pharmaceuticals was up 18 percent from 1.7 billion francs, thanks mainly to the success in the U.S. of its Luvox anti-depressant drug.
Luvox should be launched in Japan at the end of 1998, Solvay said.

Like-for-like pharmaceutical sales were up 12 percent at 20.1 billion francs. Chemicals sales were steady at 49.2 billion francs, plastics were up 31 percent at 55.2 billions, while processing sales were up five percent at 29.3 billions.

The company said it believed caustic soda prices had now bottomed and was confident of pushing through price rises this month and in September, but that there was little end in sight to the capacity price war that had hit its peroxygens business, mainly in Europe.
"We live in such erratic times, whether with products or currencies or economies, that we don't want to make the slightest comment on the second half at this stage," Janssen said.
In 1996 Solvay made a full-year profit of 13.63 billion francs, up from 12.51 billion francs in 1995 thanks mainly to a 2.09 billion franc capital gain on the animal health sale.

Separately, the company said day-to-day management would pass outside the founding Solvay family next June for the first time in its 135-year history when Janssen, 62, would step down to take over as chairman.
He will be succeeded as CEO by his current deputy, Alois Michielsen, 55, a chemist by training who has been with the company for 28 years. ($ = 37.88 Belgian Francs)
